title: microburst-waveform-latency-cost-slate-2029-05-04
body:
Purpose:
This sketch captures a compact lab sweep comparing latency percentile behavior and incremental cost under short 'microburst' traffic shapes that we observed in customer telemetry. The goal is to produce a reproducible short-form artifact that product, SRE, and runtime can iterate on. This is intentionally informal: notes, ASCII charts, and quick recommendations rather than polished slides.

Experiment summary (one-line):
- Injected synthetic microbursts (10s–90s waveforms) across three serving configs; measured token-level p50/p90/p99 and amortized dollars per 1k requests; captured warm/cold transitions and tail reverberation.

Why this matters:
- Customers see short-lived surges (chat app openers, ad-hoc search bursts) that are expensive at p99 but short enough that sustained autoscaling doesn't make sense. Understanding how small tweaks to handshake, prewarm, and batching change the shape of the tail helps prioritize product knobs.

Testbed and harness:
- Model: open-llama-13b-equivalent (quantized sim) running on a mixed GPU pool (A100-sim nodes).
- Traffic: baseline steady-state QPS=10; bursts add +120 QPS for durations [8s, 30s, 75s].
- Request mix: 70% short queries (avg tokens 32), 30% medium (avg tokens 128).
- Routing: single-region; no fallback variant during runs (to isolate waveform effect).
- Metric grab: client-observed latency (ms), server p95/99 internal, and cost meter (GPU-time amortized to $/1k requests using internal rate card).
- Runs: 8 runs per config per waveform duration; warm-run vs cold-run distinguished by idle period >= 10m.

Config matrix:
- Config A: conservative prewarm (idle-prewarm threshold 20s), batching window 10ms, small batch cap 8 tokens
- Config B: opportunistic (prewarm 2s), batching window 25ms, batch cap 32 tokens
- Config C: aggressive slot-tiling (prewarm 2s), window 10ms, tiling enabled (pack multiple sessions into a slot)

Notes on what each knob changes (short):
- Prewarm: reduces handshake and kernel priming penalties on sudden QPS jumps.
- Batching window: trades latency for packing efficiency.
- Tiling: increases multiplexing density at cost of higher p50 for single-session flows but reduces $/request for high-cardinality bursts.

Representative text-table (median across runs, warm runs):
| Config | Burst dur | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | $/1k reqs | delta $ vs A |
|--------|-----------|---------:|--------:|--------:|----------:|------------:|
| A      | 8s        |      78  |    230  |   640   |   3.9     |    0.0     |
| B      | 8s        |      95  |    270  |   980   |   3.0     |  -0.9     |
| C      | 8s        |     120  |    260  |   720   |   2.1     |  -1.8     |
| A      | 30s       |      80  |    240  |   700   |   3.6     |    0.0     |
| B      | 30s       |     110  |    300  |  1600   |   3.0     |  -0.6     |
| C      | 30s       |     135  |    285  |   820   |   2.3     |  -1.3     |
| A      | 75s       |      82  |    248  |   880   |   3.2     |    0.0     |
| B      | 75s       |     140  |    420  |  4200   |   3.4     |  +0.2     |
| C      | 75s       |     160  |    320  |  1100   |   2.5     |  -0.7     |

Key patterns (raw read):
- Short microbursts (8s): tiling (C) yields the biggest $ savings with moderate p50 increase but p99 is comparable to A. B has lower $ than A but much worse p99.
- Medium bursts (30s): B's larger batch cap helps $ but risks p99 blowups from kernel contention; C stays cheaper with more stable tails.
- Long bursts (75s): B shifts from cheap to more expensive at p99 (observed large tail events due to batch accumulation + kernel queuing); C remains cost-effective while keeping p99 lower than B but higher than A.

ASCII waveform + cost sketch (8s burst, warm run):
Time ->   0s          2s         4s         6s         8s
QPS  ->   10---++++++++++++++++++-------10-------
Latency -> p99  200     650    980     700     250  (ms)
$ density -> |====A====|==B==|===C===|   (relative $/sec, C lowest)

Behavioral observations (engineer notes):
- Batching window increase in B lets more requests pack, lowering per-token GPU-time, but occasionally forms a large batch that triggers long decode tails when KV cache misses happen at the same moment. This appears as very high p99s but not persistent.
- Tiling (C) smooths per-slot utilization and prevents individual sessions from monopolizing a fast path; it increases p50 but reduces tail multiplicative effects because contention is distributed.
- A (conservative prewarm) is better at single-session latency but expensive because reserved work slots stay underutilized during short bursts.

Operational caveats:
- Cost model assumes uniform $/GPU-hour; heterogenous fleet or spot pricing will change absolute $ numbers but relative deltas held across trials.
- These runs are single-region and single-model; multi-variant routing (fallback to smaller quantized model) was intentionally excluded. Adding fallback typically reduces p99 but increases downstream complexity and occasional hallucination-quality tradeoffs.

Recommendations (actionable):
1) For products with many short microbursts (session openers, ephemeral UIs): adopt tiling-first policy (C-like) with conservative slot caps. The tradeoff: slightly higher p50 but 30–45% $ savings on short bursts and fewer p99 catastrophes versus opportunistic batching.
2) For latency-sensitive premium tiers: maintain conservative prewarm (A) but introduce transient tiling under burst detection to avoid runaway p99s.
3) Add an automated probe in Console that detects rising batch-size variance and recommends switching to tiling mode or reducing batching window. Surface the current batch-size distribution in the call graph.
4) Expand this microburst harness to include model-variant fallbacks in the next sweep; log quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE or synthetic heuristics) to estimate accuracy-cost trade.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- How does tenant isolation change when tiling mixes low- and high-priority sessions? Need tenant-level fairness bench.
- What is the threshold burst duration where opportunistic batching becomes strictly better than tiling across realistic token mixes? (estimate: 40–60s; run systematic sweep)
- Are there kernel-level mitigations (stream-level priorities) that reduce B's p99 without killing its $ advantages?

Appendix (quick run checklist for reproducing locally):
- branch: benchmarks/microburst-waveform (PR linked above)
- run script: ./run_waveform_sweep.sh --model open-13b-q --durations 8,30,75 --configs A,B,C --seed 42 --collect client,server --persist results/*.csv
- postproc: python tools/plot_waveform_ascii.py results/*.csv

TL;DR (one-paragraph):
Short microbursts expose a triage: reserved prewarm (A) preserves low-latency but costs more; opportunistic batching (B) reduces $ in many steady cases but can produce very high p99s when large batches coincide with cache churn; tiling (C) offers a middle ground that is the most cost-effective for sub-minute bursts at the expense of slightly higher median latency. Recommendation is to expose tiling as the default for ephemeral-traffic products and build a console probe to flip policies automatically when batch variance rises.

Notes-to-self: convert this into a 1-page customer-facing briefing and a companion playground script for SRE. Save raw CSVs under GDrive bench results for audit.
